summary:
Aruba stands under the national framework of the Netherlands and applies its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012. The Code prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social, cultural or other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 punish such discrimination and incitement with fines and imprisonment up to one year. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed in the enumerated grounds.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba for both male and female conduct. The age of consent is 16 and is equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands, which upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. A prior ruling of 13 April 2007 by the Dutch Supreme Court had required Aruba to recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, after the Aruban government refused recognition to a lesbian couple married in the Netherlands.

Registered partnerships open to both same-sex and opposite-sex couples have been available since the parliamentary vote of 8 September 2016 extending civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions. The regime confers spousal pension rights and emergency medical decision rights. Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide before that vote.

Commercial provision for LGBT visitors is widespread. Venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly across the island, with several specific gay bars and clubs concentrated as an example in the capital city of Oranjestad. No documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically was provided, and no transgender-specific facts on facilities, screening, custody, care or protection were provided.
tangentialFactors:
The official tourism board markets Aruba as an established LGBT destination and presents feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering. It quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. That account is self-description by the destination marketer, not independent evidence.

A 2017 cultural report described Aruba as tolerant and mostly open, with a smaller and quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao. Aruba was described at the time as the first island in the Caribbean to adopt registered partnerships, while neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed such unions.

Local advocacy sources describe public acceptance as conditional and discreet. The Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba is quoted as stating that Aruba has always been accepting as long as it is not in their face, that people are out but discreetly out, and that there has never been anything official.

The government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands. It was vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during the 2004-2007 court challenge that required Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. Religious and cultural opposition to the 2016 partnership bill was strong. The Roman Catholic Church, as the largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights and same-sex marriage, with Catholic influence described as the main brake.

Lesbian litigants Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during that 2004-2007 challenge. All tolerance, venue, association, harassment and opposition observations concern LGBT people generally or same-sex couples specifically.
localsOnly:
The registered partnership law followed a 2.5-year campaign. The bill was introduced on 22 August 2016 by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes and passed on 8 September 2016 by 11 votes to 5 with four abstentions. An Igualdad Aruba petition gathered nearly 20,000 signatures. The sponsor had herself used the Netherlands marriage route that was already recognized kingdom-wide.

A separate same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tie votes in May and June 2024, before marriage was established by court ruling in July 2024.

Same-sex adoption is legal.

Several LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, with marriage litigation supported by Fundacion Orguyo Aruba.
